Supporting volume rotation with light from a fixed direction is difficult because the light direction relative to the volume changes as the volume rotates, while the slicing planes and texture mapping are view-dependent [S1].

The claim states that supporting volume rotation with light from a fixed direction is difficult because the light direction relative to the volume changes as it rotates, while slicing planes and texture mapping are view-dependent. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 3.1.5 Summary: 'For example, supporting volume rotation with light shining from a fixed direction is quite difficult with volume slicing.' Additionally, the notes and passages explain that volume slicing relies on planes parallel to the projection plane (view-dependent) and texture mapping, which creates the difficulty when the volume rotates relative to a fixed light source.

# Render planes back-to-front [S1, S2, S3]

All three sources explicitly state that volume slicing techniques involve rendering parallel planes (or proxy geometry) in a back-to-front order (often alongside front-to-back) to composite the final image. Source [S1] states 'rendering the planes back-to-front', Source [S2] mentions 'slicing the dataset in front-to-back or back-to-front order', and Source [S3] states 'rendered in front-to-back or back-to-front order'.
supported
It is distinguished from other object-order methods by its direct use of graphics hardware for both data storage and sampling, avoiding software rendering bottlenecks [S1, S3].

The claim states that the method is distinguished by its direct use of graphics hardware for data storage (3D texture maps) and sampling (texture lookups via parallel planes), which avoids software rendering bottlenecks. Source [S1] explicitly describes this technique as 'hardware-accelerated direct volume rendering' where voxels are stored in a '3D texture map' and rendered by slicing with planes that perform 'texture lookups' using '3D texturing hardware'. It further notes that this approach is 'faster than software-based direct volume rendering' and enables 'real-time interactivity by avoiding software rendering bottlenecks'. Source [S3] corroborates this by defining 'Texture Slicing' as an object-space method that maps volume to '2D or 3D textures in graphics hardware' and notes that object-space approaches are 'fast and efficient for modern graphics processors' and the 'choice for interactivity'. Both sources confirm that the use of hardware for storage and sampling distinguishes this method from software-based alternatives by improving performance and avoiding bottlenecks.
supported

This confirms that the accumulation process utilizes linear alpha blending.

Progressive refinement is supported by initially rendering a few slices and improving resolution over time, and users may request dynamic slicing perpendicular to any viewing direction [S4].

The claim is fully supported by the text in Source [S4], specifically within Section 5 ('Plane Slicing'). The text explicitly states: 'Images may be generated using progressive refinement: initially a few slices are rendered, then as time permits the resolution of the image is improved by rendering it with more slices.' It also states: 'For any viewing direction, the user may request that a new set of slices be generated perpendicular to that direction.' Both parts of the claim are directly present in the evidence.

The graphics hardware interpolates texture coordinates across each plane, performs texture lookups, and accumulates colors and opacities using linear alpha blending to composite the final image [S1, S3].

The claim is fully supported by the evidence. Source [S1] explicitly states that 'the graphics subsystem interpolates texture coordinates across the area of each individual plane, performing the appropriate texture lookup at each location' and that the final image is created by 'accumulating colours and opacities in a compositing step.' It further specifies that 'Linear alpha blending, used by the rendering system for compositing, requires that the parallel polygons be rendered from back to front.' Source [S3] corroborates this by describing texture slicing as a method where parallel planes slice the volume and are 'rendered in front-to-back or back-to-front order and composited into a the resulting image.' All specific technical details in the claim (interpolation, lookups, accumulation, linear alpha blending, back-to-front compositing) are present in the provided sources.
